title: Automated versus Manual Impaction in Total Hip Replacement: Implications for Patient Rehabilitation
summary:
Background: When an artificial hip joint is implanted, the components must be firmly anchored in the bone. This is done either by hand with a mallet or with a new automated device. Whether the automated device helps patients recover faster and better after surgery has not yet been well studied.
Research question: We want to find out whether walking ability, mobility and quality of life recover better after surgery when the automated device is used instead of the mallet.
Methodology: 48 patients are randomly assigned to one of the two groups. Walking is measured in the gait laboratory before surgery and about three weeks and three months afterwards; patients also complete questionnaires on symptoms and quality of life. These assessments take place at already scheduled appointments. Some participants additionally take part in interviews about their personal experience of recovery.

interventions.name: Intervention group (n = 24): primary, unilateral, cementless total hip arthroplasty in which femoral broaching and cup impaction are performed with the automated impaction system (DePuy Synthes KINCISE). Approach, implant and rehabilitation are standardised. Assessments at T0 (day before surgery), T

Control group (n = 24): identical primary, unilateral, cementless total hip arthroplasty in which femoral broaching and cup impaction are performed fully manually with a standard surgical mallet. Approach, implant, rehabilitation and all measurement/assessment time points (T0, T1, T2) are identical
